analysis.one_liner: Opens unused TV broadcast channels to free, unlicensed wireless broadband use.
analysis.headline: The bill, which let wireless devices use vacant TV channels to expand broadband, was introduced with bipartisan support in April 2006 and never left committee before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill ordered the government to let anyone use television channels that are assigned to stations but not actually being used — the gaps in the broadcast band. Wireless internet providers, especially in rural areas, could use this free public spectrum to reach homes that cable and phone companies don't serve. The FCC would write rules to keep the devices from interfering with TV broadcasts and public safety radios.
analysis.who_benefits: Rural and underserved communities that lack wired broadband, since low-frequency TV signals travel long distances and pass through walls cheaply. Small wireless internet companies and equipment makers also gain, because unlicensed spectrum is free to use. Consumers generally gain access to a new, cheaper way to get online.
analysis.who_pays: Broadcast television stations and other licensed users of the TV band give up exclusive control over the channels they hold but don't use, and they carry the burden of proving interference complaints. Equipment makers pay certification costs. Taxpayers lose nothing; the spectrum simply goes from being reserved to being shared.
analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — free access to vacant public airwaves for broadband where wired service is expensive or absent — is real and large for the people affected, which is why similar 'white spaces' rules were later adopted by the FCC in 2008. The cost is concentrated on broadcasters, who risk interference into a service many households still depended on in 2006. The bill tried to manage that risk with interference rules, device certification, and 30-day complaint handling, but early device technology was unproven, so the broadcasters' concern was not baseless.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its telecommunications subcommittee until the Congress ended, with no markup and no floor vote ever scheduled.
outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Television broadcasters kept their exclusive claim on every channel they held, including idle ones, and unlicensed wireless broadband devices got no access to the TV band during this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all four cosponsors split evenly between the parties — two Democrats and two Republicans introduced it together, and no vote on it was ever recorded.

industries.note: Broadcasters would share the TV band, losing exclusive rights to channels they held but did not use, and would bear the burden of proving interference complaints. Their interest in keeping the band to themselves ran against communities that wanted the idle spectrum for broadband.

industries.industry: Wireless internet providers and unlicensed device makers
industries.note: Free access to low-frequency TV spectrum would let small wireless ISPs and equipment makers reach customers, especially rural ones, at low cost. The bill required device certification and remote-remedy plans, a modest regulatory cost.
